lesson.title: Boundary and area

lead.text: Take the tiling first. A tile is a square and every tile is the same size, so tiles laid edge to edge, with no gaps and no overlaps, cover a floor completely. The number of tiles it takes measures how much floor there is. That amount is called the area of the floor, and it is counted in unit squares. If each tile is 1 metre across, a tile is a square metre, written 1 m², and a floor that takes 12 tiles has an area of 12 m².

Counting tiles one at a time is slow. Tiles lie in rows, and every row has the same number of tiles. A floor with 4 rows of 8 tiles holds 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32 tiles, which is 4 × 8. So the area of a rectangle is the number of rows times the number of tiles in each row, and that is the same as its length times its width.

afterFigure.text: The small 2 in m² records that the unit is a square with a metre along each side.

lead.text: Count with the rows, not one tile at a time.

Now the skirting board. It runs along the bottom of every wall, so the length you need is the distance all the way round the edge of the room. That distance is the perimeter of a shape. You find it by adding the lengths of all the sides, and it is measured in ordinary units of length such as metres.

A rectangle has a helpful pattern, because its opposite sides are equal. A room 9 m long and 3 m wide has two walls of 9 m and two walls of 3 m, so its perimeter is 9 + 3 + 9 + 3 = 24 m. You can shorten the sum to 2 × (9 + 3), which counts two lengths and two widths. Either way the unit is metres, since a perimeter is a distance.

afterFigure.text: The room now has a perimeter and an area, and both come from the same two numbers. Next, a 6 m by 4 m room needs both.

steps.headline: A room is 6 m by 4 m. Find its perimeter and its area.

workedSteps.text: Add all four sides for the skirting board.

lead.text: Perimeter and area both come from the same two sides, but they do not move together. Take two rooms that each need 16 m of skirting board. One is 4 m by 4 m. The other is a long strip, 7 m by 1 m.

Add the sides and each perimeter is 16 m: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 for the square and 7 + 1 + 7 + 1 for the strip. Now count tiles. The square has 4 rows of 4, which is 16 tiles. The strip has 1 row of 7, which is 7 tiles.

Both rooms have the same distance round them, yet the square takes more than twice as many tiles. Once the perimeter is fixed, the shape decides the area. The two measures answer different questions, and a number for one tells you little about the other.
Add up the sides round each rectangle, then count the squares inside it.

Many everyday problems come down to choosing between the two measures. A fence, a picture frame or a border runs along an edge, so each needs a perimeter. Paint, turf, carpet and tiles cover a surface, so each needs an area. Asking whether the job goes round the edge or across the inside settles it.

The unit shows which measure an answer is. A perimeter is a length, so it is written in units such as metres. An area counts squares, so it is written in square units such as m². Always write the unit with the answer, since a bare 24 could be either. The figure shows one room measured both ways.

diagram.alt: A rectangular room 8 metres by 3 metres drawn as a grid of tiles. One view traces the edge in bold for a perimeter job such as a fence. The other fills the inside for an area job such as paint or tiles.
diagram.caption: The same room, measured two ways. The edge gives a length in metres and the inside gives an area in square metres.

lead.text: Count the squares row by row.

So far the sides have come first and the area second. A problem can run the other way. A tiler knows a floor takes 40 tiles and that one wall is 5 tiles long. The puzzle is the length of the other wall.

The area is the number of rows times the number of tiles in each row, so 40 = 5 × (the other side). Division undoes multiplying, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so the other wall is 8 tiles long. Whenever you know the area and one side of a rectangle, divide the area by that side to find the other.
One more idea needs both measures together: a fixed amount of fence and a choice of shape for the garden it surrounds.

diagram.alt: A floor 5 tiles wide with 40 tiles in all. The first view marks the number of rows as unknown. The second divides 40 by 5 to show there are 8 rows.
diagram.caption: Dividing the area by the known side gives the other side.

lead.text: Two lengths and two widths make 20 m of fence, so one length and one width add to 10 m. The sides must be whole numbers.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish distance around a shape from the surface it covers.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You have bought a flat with an empty rectangular room, and two jobs need doing. Skirting board has to run along the bottom of every wall, and the floor has to be tiled from wall to wall. The same room goes into both jobs, but they ask for different amounts.

The skirting board is sold by the metre, so you need a length: how far it is round the room. The tiles are sold by the box, so you need a count: how many fit on the floor. Two rooms can need the same length of skirting board and very different numbers of tiles.
This lesson takes the two jobs one at a time and then puts them side by side. By the end you can tell which measurement a problem is asking for and work out both for any rectangle.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell the distance round a rectangle from the space inside it, and find both.

recap.keyIdea: Perimeter is the distance round a shape and area counts the squares inside. For a rectangle, add all four sides for the first and multiply the two sides for the second.

blocks.text: Back in the room, you counted 15 tiles in 3 rows of 5 and then worked out the skirting board for rooms of different shapes.
You found that 6 by 4 and 8 by 2 rectangles share a perimeter but not an area, and that 20 m of fence can enclose up to 25 m².

recap.nextHook: Rectangles are easy to count in rows. A card cut corner to corner leaves two triangles with a slanting edge, and the next lesson works out which length to use for them.

questions.prompt: Rectangle A is 6 m by 4 m and rectangle B is 8 m by 2 m. Which statement is true?
hints: Add the sides round each rectangle.
Count the rows of squares in each, then the squares per row.
Compare the two boundary totals, then the two square counts.

acceptedIdeas: They have the same perimeter but different areas
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both perimeters are 20, while their areas are 24 and 16 square units.

choices.label: They have the same perimeter but different areas
They have the same area but different perimeters
They have equal areas and equal perimeters

questions.onCorrect: Equal perimeters can hide different areas. Add the sides for one, count squares for the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Add the four sides of each rectangle. Do the two totals really differ?
Count the squares in each rectangle. Do they hold the same number?

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide.
hints: Perimeter is the total boundary.
There are two sides of each length.
Calculate 2 × (6 + 4).
questions.onCorrect: Perimeter adds all four sides. Opposite sides are equal, so two of each length.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 6 × 4, the area. Perimeter is the distance round the edge.
That's 6 + 4, only half the boundary. Count all four sides.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide, in square units.
hints: Count square units inside the boundary.
Use the number of rows and squares in each row.
Multiply 6 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six squares per row across four rows give 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

questions.onCorrect: Area counts squares inside: 4 rows of 6, so 6 × 4, in square units.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the distance round the edge. Area counts the squares inside.
That adds 6 + 4. Area multiplies rows by squares in each row.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 7 units by 3 units. What area does it cover in square units?
hints: Area counts the inside.
Multiply the two perpendicular dimensions.
Calculate 7 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 21 square units. Rows times squares per row gives the area of any rectangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the distance round the edge. Area counts the squares inside.
That adds 7 + 3. Area multiplies the two sides.

questions.prompt: A rectangular floor has area 54 m² and width 6 m. Find its length in metres.
hints: Area is length times width.
Undo multiplication by the known width.
Divide 54 by 6.
questions.onCorrect: 9 m. Area is length × width, so divide the area by the width to undo it.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 54 by 6. Division undoes multiplying.
That takes 6 away. The area is the length times 6, so undo the multiplying.

questions.prompt: Which unit is appropriate for the area of a small floor?
hints: A unit square has both length and width.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Area counts two-dimensional coverage, so it uses square metres.

questions.onCorrect: Square metres. Area counts squares, so it is measured in squares of a length unit.

misconceptions.feedback: Metres measure a length. Area counts squares.
Cubic metres measure space with three directions. A floor's cover has two.

questions.prompt: A floor is covered in square tiles: 3 rows, with 5 tiles in each row. How many tiles cover the floor?
hints: Picture one row. How many tiles is that?
How many rows are there?

questions.onCorrect: 15. Three rows of 5 tiles: counting squares in equal rows is multiplying.

questions.prompt: You are putting a fence round a garden. Which measurement do you need?
hints: Does a fence cover the inside or go round the edge?
questions.onCorrect: The perimeter. A fence runs along the edge, so you need the distance round it.

questions.prompt: A gardener has 20 m of fence for a rectangular garden with whole-number sides. What is the largest area she can enclose, in square metres?
hints: The length and width add to 10 m. List pairs that do.
Work out the area of each pair.
Which pair has sides closest together?
questions.onCorrect: 25 m². Same fence, different shapes: the more even the sides, the more space inside.

misconceptions.feedback: 24 m² is the 6 by 4 garden. Try pairs of sides that are closer together.
20 is the length of the fence. Find the area inside it.

questions.prompt: A field is 12 m long and 5 m wide. Find the distance all the way round it, in metres.
hints: Opposite sides are equal. How many sides are 12 m long?
Add both pairs of sides.
questions.onCorrect: 34 m. The perimeter adds all four sides, two of each length.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 12 × 5, the area. The distance round is a sum of sides.
That's 12 + 5, only half the way round. There are two of each side.
